As the\\\\nrate increases and the queuing delay (second term) becomes\\\\nmore significant, inter-op parallelism becomes advantageous,\\\\nconcurred with Figure 4(a).\\\\nThe prefill phase’s preference for parallelism is also influ-\\\\nenced by TTFT SLO and the speedup coefficient K. Seen\\\\nfrom Figure 4(a): A more stringent SLO will make intra-op\\\\nparallelism more advantageous, due to its ability to reduce\\\\nexecution time. The value of K depends on factors such as the\\\\ninput length, model architecture, communication bandwidth,\\\\nand placement [46,59]. As shown in Figure 4(b), a decrease in\\\\nK notably reduces the efficacy of intra-op parallelism. §4 de-\\\\nvelops algorithms that optimize the resource and parallelism\\\\nconfigurations taking into consideration these knobs.\\\\n3.2\\\\nAnalysis for Decoding Instance\\\\nUnlike the prefill instance, a decoding instance follows a dis-\\\\ntinct computational pattern: it receives the KV caches and\\\\nthe first output token from the prefill instance and generates\\\\nsubsequent tokens one at a time. For decoding instances, our\\\\noptimization goal is to satisfy the application’s TPOT require-\\\\nment using minimal computing resources.\\\\nBatching strategy. Since a single decoding job is heav-\\\\nily bandwidth-bound, batching is key to avoiding low GPU\\\\nutilization (hence high per-gpu goodput), as shown in Fig-\\\\nure 3(b). In existing systems where the prefill and decoding\\\\nphases are colocated, increasing the decoding batch size is\\\\ndifficult because it conflicts with meeting latency goals, par-\\\\nticularly in scenarios with high request rates. This is because\\\\nsharing GPUs cause competition between prefill and decod-\\\\ning jobs, leading to a trade-off between TTFT and TPOT. For\\\\n5\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 6 ---\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n8\\\\n#GPUs\\\\n30\\\\n40\\\\n50\\\\n60\\\\nLatency (ms)\\\\n0\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n8\\\\n#GPUs\\\\n0\\\\n5000\\\\n10000\\\\n15000\\\\nThroughput (tokens/s)\\\\nLinear Scaling\\\\nInter-op\\\\nIntra-op\\\\nFigure 5: Decoding phase latency and throughput when serv-\\\\ning a 13B LLM with batch size = 128 and input length = 256\\\\nunder different parallel degrees.\\\\nexample, a higher arrival rate generates more prefill jobs, de-\\\\nmanding greater GPU time to meet TTFT requirements if\\\\nprioritizing prefill jobs, which in turn adversely affects TPOT.\\\\nOn the contrary, disaggregation offers a solution by en-\\\\nabling the allocation of multiple prefill instances to a single\\\\ndecoding instance. This approach allows for accumulating a\\\\nlarger batch size on dedicated GPUs for the decoding phase\\\\nwithout sacrificing TPOT.\\\\nParallelism plan. Post-disaggregation, the batch size for de-\\\\ncoding may be constrained by GPU memory capacity, as it is\\\\nnecessary to maintain the KV caches for all active requests.\\\\nScaling the decoding instance with model parallelism or lever-\\\\naging advanced memory management techniques for LLM\\\\nKV caches, such as Paged-Attention [32] and GQA [10],\\\\nenable further scaling of the decoding batch size to nearly\\\\ncompute-bound. As the decoding batch size continue to in-\\\\ncrease to approach the compute-bound, the decoding compu-\\\\ntation begins to resemble the prefill phase. With this observa-\\\\ntion, we investigate how the latency and throughput change\\\\nunder different parallelism degrees under large batch condi-\\\\ntions in Figure 5: intra-op parallelism reduces latency with\\\\ndiminishing returns, caused by communication and reduced\\\\nutilization after partitioning. Inter-op parallelism can almost\\\\nlinearly scale the throughput. Hence, when the TPOT SLO\\\\nis stringent, intra-op parallelism is essential to reduce TPOT\\\\nto meet latency goals. Beyond this, inter-op parallelism is\\\\npreferable to enhance throughput linearly.\\\\nIt is worth noting that when the model can fit into the mem-\\\\nory of a single GPU, replication is a competitive option in\\\\naddition to model parallelism for both prefill and decoding\\\\ninstances, to linearly scale the system’s rate capacity. It may\\\\nalso reduce the queuing delay – as indicated by Eq. 1 – by\\\\nsubstituting R with R/N assuming requests are equally dis-\\\\npatched to N replicas, at the cost of maintaining additional\\\\nreplicas of the model weights in GPU memory.\\\\n3.3\\\\nPractical Problems\\\\nWe have developed foundational principles for selecting batch-\\\\ning and parallelisms for each phase. In this section, we discuss\\\\nand address several challenges encountered during the practi-\\\\ncal deployment of disaggregated prefill and decoding phases.\\\\nVariable prefill length. §3 has assumed uniform prompt\\\\nlength across requests. In real deployments, depending on\\\\nthe LLM application, the lengths of requests are non-uniform.\\\\nThe non-uniformity can cause pipeline bubbles [28,36] for\\\\nprefill instances applying inter-op parallelism because the\\\\nexecution time of pipeline stages across requests of different\\\\nlengths will vary. This results in slight deviations from the\\\\nconclusions indicated by using the M/D/1 queue model. To\\\\naddress the problem, §4 develops algorithms that search for\\\\nparallelisms based on workloads, and resort to scheduling to\\\\nminimize the bubbles (§4.3).\\\\nCommunication overhead. Transferring KV caches from\\\\nprefill to decoding instances incurs notable overheads. For\\\\nexample, the KV cache size of a single 512-token request\\\\non OPT-66B is approximately 1.13GB. Assuming an aver-\\\\nage arrival rate of 10 rps, we need to transfer 11.3GB data\\\\nper second—or equivalently 90Gbps bandwidth to render the\\\\noverhead invisible. While many modern GPU clusters for\\\\nLLMs are equipped with InfiniBand (e.g., 800 Gbps), in cases\\\\nwhere cross-node bandwidth is limited, DistServe relies on\\\\nthe commonly available intra-node NVLINK, where the peak\\\\nbandwidth between A100 GPUs is 600 GB/s, again rendering\\\\nthe transmission overhead negligible (see §6.3). However, this\\\\nrequirement imposes additional constraints on the placement\\\\nof prefill and decoding instances that we take into considera-\\\\ntion in the next section.\\\\nThrough the analysis in this section, we identify the work-\\\\nload pattern, placement constraints, SLO requirements, paral-\\\\nlelism strategies, and resource allocation as key parameters\\\\nthat create a web of considerations in designing the disag-\\\\ngregated serving system. How to automatically navigate the\\\\nsearch space to find the configuration that achieves optimal\\\\nper-gpu goodput is challenging, and addressed next.\\\\n4\\\\nMethod\\\\nWe built DistServe to solve the above challenges. Given the\\\\nmodel, workload characteristic, latency requirements, and\\\\nSLO attainment target, DistServe will determine (a) the par-\\\\nallelism strategies for prefill and decoding instances, (b) the\\\\nnumber of each instance type to deploy, as well as (c) how\\\\nto place them onto the physical cluster. We call the solution\\\\na placement. Our goal is to find a placement that maximizes\\\\nthe per-gpu goodput.\\\\nAs explained in §3.3, a key design consideration is to man-\\\\nage communications between disaggregated prefill and de-\\\\ncoding phases, given varying cluster setups. In this section,\\\\nwe first present two placement algorithms: one for clusters\\\\nwith high-speed cross-node networks (§4.1) and the other\\\\nfor environments lacking such infrastructure (§4.2); the lat-\\\\nter introduces additional constraints. We then develop online\\\\nscheduling optimizations that adapt to the nuances of real-\\\\nworld workloads (§4.3).\\\\n6\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 7 ---\\\\nAlgorithm 1 High Node-Affinity Placement Algorithm\\\\nInput: LLM G, #node limit per-instance N, #GPU per-node\\\\nM, GPU memory capacity C, workload W, traffic rate R.\\\\nOutput: the placement best_plm.\\\\nconfigp,configd ←/0, /0\\\\nfor intra_op ∈{1,2,...,M} do\\\\nfor inter_op ∈{1,2,...,\\\\nN×M\\\\nintra_op} do\\\\nif\\\\nG.size\\\\ninter_op×intra_op < C then\\\\nconfig ←(inter_op,intra_op)\\\\nˆG ←parallel(G,config)\\\\nconfig.goodput ←simu_prefill( ˆG,W)\\\\nif\\\\nconfigp.goodput\\\\ncon figp.num_gpus <\\\\nconfig.goodput\\\\ncon fig.num_gpus then\\\\nconfigp ←config\\\\nconfig.goodput ←simu_decode( ˆG,W)\\\\nif\\\\nconfigd.goodput\\\\ncon figd.num_gpus <\\\\nconfig.goodput\\\\ncon fig.num_gpus then\\\\nconfigd ←config\\\\nn,m ←⌈\\\\nR\\\\nconfigp.goodput⌉,⌈\\\\nR\\\\nconfigd.goodput⌉\\\\nbest_plm ←(n,configp,m,configd)\\\\nreturn best_plm\\\\n4.1\\\\nPlacement for High Node-Affinity Cluster\\\\nOn high node-affinity clusters equipped with Infiniband, KV\\\\ncaches transmission overhead across nodes is negligible, Dist-\\\\nServe can deploy prefill and decoding instances across any\\\\ntwo nodes without constraints. We propose a two-level place-\\\\nment algorithm for such scenarios: we first optimize the par-\\\\nallelism configurations for prefill and decoding instances sep-\\\\narately to attain phase-level optimal per-gpu goodput; then,\\\\nwe use replication to match the overall traffic rate.\\\\nHowever, finding the optimal parallel configuration for a\\\\nsingle instance type, such as for the prefill instance, is still\\\\nchallenging, due to the lack of a simple analytical formula to\\\\ncalculate the SLO attainment (a.k.a., percentage of requests\\\\nthat meet TTFT requirement), given that the workload has\\\\ndiverse input, output lengths, and irregular arrival patterns.\\\\nGauging the SLO via real-testbed profiling is time-prohibitive.\\\\nWe thus resort to building a simulator to estimate the SLO at-\\\\ntainment, assuming prior knowledge of the workload’s arrival\\\\nprocess and input and output length distributions. Although\\\\nshort-term interval is impossible to predict, the workload\\\\npattern over longer timescales (e.g., hours or days) is often\\\\npredictable [33, 55]. DistServe fits a distribution from the\\\\nhistory request traces and resamples new traces from the dis-\\\\ntribution as the input workload to the simulator to compute\\\\nthe SLO attainment. Next, DistServe simply enumerates the\\\\nplacements and finds the maximum rate that meets the SLO\\\\nattainment target with binary search and simulation trials.\\\\nAlgorithm 1 outlines the process. We enumerate all feasible\\\\nparallel configurations, subject to cluster capacity limit, for\\\\nboth prefill and decoding instances. Then, for a specific pre-\\\\nfill phase configuration, we use simu_prefill to simulate\\\\nAlgorithm 2 Low Node-Affinity Placement Algorithm\\\\nInput: LLM G, #node limit per-instance N, #GPU per-node\\\\nM, GPU memory capacity C, workload W, traffic rate R.\\\\nOutput: the placement best_plm.\\\\nconfig∗←/0\\\\nfor inter_op ∈{1,2,...,N} do\\\\nP ←get_intra_node_configs(G,M,C,inter_op)\\\\nfor Pp ∈P do\\\\nfor Pd ∈P do\\\\nif Pp.num_gpus+Pd.num_gpus ≤M then\\\\nconfig ←(inter_op,Pp,Pd)\\\\nˆGp, ˆGd ←parallel(G,config)\\\\nconfig.goodput ←simulate( ˆGp, ˆGd,W)\\\\nif\\\\nconfig.∗goodput\\\\nconfig.∗num_gpus <\\\\nconfig.goodput\\\\nconfig.num_gpus then\\\\nconfig∗←config\\\\nn ←⌈\\\\nR\\\\nconfig.∗goodput⌉\\\\nbest_plm ←(n,config∗)\\\\nreturn best_plm\\\\nand find its maximum goodput via binary search (similarly\\\\nfor using simu_decode for decoding). After determining the\\\\noptimal parallel configurations for both prefill and decoding\\\\ninstances, we replicate them to achieve the user-required over-\\\\nall traffic rate according to their goodput.\\\\nThe complexity of Algorithm 1 is O(NM2), with N as the\\\\nnode limit per instance and M representing the typical number\\\\nof GPUs per node in modern clusters (e.g., 8). The search\\\\nspace is manageable and the solving time is under 1.3 minutes\\\\nin our largest setting, as demonstrated in §6.5.\\\\nSimulator building. Algorithm 1 relies on a simulator to es-\\\\ntimate the goodput under various SLOs and SLO attainment\\\\ngoals given the workload and the parallelism plan. To build an\\\\naccurate simulator, we analyze the FLOPs and the number of\\\\nmemory accesses for prefill and decoding phases respectively,\\\\nand use a latency model to approximate the inference execu-\\\\ntion time. See details in Appendix A. The simulator aligns\\\\nwell with real profiling results, thanks to the high predictabil-\\\\nity of DNN workloads [23,33], verified in §6.4.\\\\nBy far, we have developed Algorithm 1 assuming we can\\\\nplace the prefill and decoding instance between any two nodes\\\\n(or on the same node) of the cluster, and the KV cache trans-\\\\nmission utilizes high bandwidth network. In many real clus-\\\\nters, GPUs inside a node access to high-bandwidth NVLINK\\\\nwhile GPUs distributed across nodes have limited bandwidth.\\\\nWe next develop an algorithm to address this constraint.\\\\n4.2\\\\nPlacement for Low Node-Affinity Cluster\\\\nA straightforward solution is to always colocate prefill and\\\\ndecoding instances on the same node, utilizing the NVLINK,\\\\nwhich is commonly available inside a GPU node. For large\\\\nmodels, e.g. with 175B parameters (350GB), we may be un-\\\\nable to even host a single pair of prefill and decoding instances\\\\n7\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 8 ---\\\\nin an 8-GPU node (80G × 8 = 640G < 350 × 2GB). We in-\\\\ncorporate this as additional placement constraints and co-\\\\noptimize it with model parallelism, presented in Algorithm 2.\\\\nThe key insight is that KV cache transfer occurs exclu-\\\\nsively between corresponding layers of prefill and decoding\\\\ninstances. Leveraging inter-op parallelism, we group layers\\\\ninto stages and divide each instance into segments, termed\\\\nas instance segments, with each segment maintaining one\\\\nspecific inter-op stage. By colocating prefill and decoding\\\\nsegments of the same stage within a single node, we force\\\\nthe transfer of intermediate states to occur only via NVLINK.\\\\nInside a node, we set the same parallelism and resource allo-\\\\ncation for segments of the same instance. Given the typical\\\\nlimitation of GPUs per node (usually 8), we can enumerate\\\\npossible configurations inside one node and use the simulator\\\\nto identify the configurations that yield the best goodput.\\\\nAs outlined in Algorithm 2, we begin by enumerating inter-\\\\nop parallelism degrees to get all the possible instance seg-\\\\nments. For each segment, we get all possible intra-node paral-\\\\nlelism configurations by calling get_intra_node_configs.\\\\nThen we use simulation to find the optimal one and replicate\\\\nit to satisfy the target traffic rate.\\\\n4.3\\\\nOnline scheduling\\\\nThe runtime architecture of DistServe is shown in Figure 6.\\\\nDistServe operates with a simple FCFS scheduling policy.\\\\nAll incoming requests arrive at a centralized controller, then\\\\ndispatched to the prefill instance with the shortest queue for\\\\nprefill processing, followed by dispatch to the least loaded de-\\\\ncoding instance for decoding steps. This setup, while simple,\\\\nis optimized with several key enhancements tailored to the\\\\nnuances of real-world workloads.\\\\nReducing pipeline bubbles. To mitigate the pipeline bubbles\\\\ncaused by non-uniform prompt lengths (§3.3), we schedule\\\\nthe requests in a way that balances the execution time across\\\\nall batches in the pipeline. This is achieved by noting that,\\\\nfor both prefill and decoding instances, the number of new\\\\ntokens in the batch is a reliable indicator of the batch’s real\\\\nexecution time. For prefill instances, we profile the target\\\\nmodel and GPU to figure out the shortest prompt length Lm\\\\nneeded to saturate the GPU. We schedule prefill batches with a\\\\ntotal sequence length close to Lm, by either batching multiple\\\\nrequests shorter than Lm or individually scheduling requests\\\\nlonger than Lm. For decoding instances, we set Lm as the\\\\nlargest batch size.\\\\nCombat busrtiness. Burstiness in workloads can cause a\\\\ndeluge of KV caches to transfer from prefill to decoding in-\\\\nstances, risking memory overload on decoding instances. To\\\\ncircumvent this, DistServe employs a “pull” method for KV\\\\ncache transmission rather than a “push” approach – decoding\\\\ninstances fetch KV cache from prefill instances as needed, us-\\\\ning the GPU memory of prefill instances as a queuing buffer.\\\\nThis way, the prefill instance can continue handling other\\\\nController\\\\nPrefill Instance\\\\nRequests\\\\nParallel Runtime\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\nLLM Model\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\nParallel Runtime\\\\nDecoding Instance\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\nLLM Model\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\nKV Cache \\\\nTransfer\\\\nParallel Runtime\\\\nFigure 6: DistServe Runtime System Architecture\\\\nprefill jobs by simply retaining the KV Cache in the GPU\\\\nmemory after processing the prompt. Hence, each type of in-\\\\nstance operates at its own pace without complex coordination.\\\\nReplaning. The resource and parallelism plan in DistServe is\\\\noptimized for a specific workload pattern, which may become\\\\nsuboptimal if the workload pattern changes over time. Dist-\\\\nServe implement periodic replanning. A workload profiler\\\\nmonitors key parameters such as the average input and output\\\\nlength of the requests, the average arrival rate, etc. If a signif-\\\\nicant pattern shift is detected, DistServe will trigger a rerun\\\\nof the placement algorithm based on recent historical data.\\\\nThis process is expedient – the proposed algorithm runs in\\\\nseconds (§6.5) and reloading LLM weights can be completed\\\\nwithin minutes – far shorter than the hourly scale at which\\\\nreal-world workload variations tend to occur.\\\\nPreemption and fault tolerance. DistServe does not imple-\\\\nment advanced runtime policies like preemption [26] and\\\\nfault tolerance [58], which are complementary to disaggre-\\\\ngation. Nevertheless, we discuss how they fit into DistServe.\\\\nIn DistServe, the FCFS policy can lead to a “convoy effect”,\\\\nwhere longer requests block shorter ones in the prefill stage.\\\\nIncorporating preemptive strategies, as suggested in existing\\\\nliterature [53], could enhance efficiency and is feasible within\\\\nour system’s architecture. While not a primary focus in the\\\\ncurrent DistServe, fault tolerance is a critical aspect for con-\\\\nsideration. In traditional colocation- and replication-based\\\\nsystems, a fault in one instance typically does not disrupt\\\\nother replica instances. However, in DistServe, the depen-\\\\ndency between prefill and decoding instances introduces the\\\\nrisk of fault propagation. For example, a fault in a single de-\\\\ncoding instance mapped to multiple prefill instances could\\\\npotentially cripple the entire service and cluster. We leave\\\\nboth as future work.\\\\n5\\\\nImplementation\\\\nDistServe is an end-to-end distributed serving system for\\\\nLLMs with a placement algorithm module, a RESTful API\\\\nfrontend, an orchestration layer, and a parallel execution en-\\\\ngine. The algorithm module, frontend, and orchestration layer\\\\nare implemented with 6.5K lines of Python code. The par-\\\\nallel execution engine is implemented with 8.1K lines of\\\\n8\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 9 ---\\\\nApplication\\\\nModel Size\\\\nTTFT\\\\nTPOT\\\\nDataset\\\\nChatbot OPT-13B\\\\n26GB\\\\n0.25s\\\\n0.1s\\\\nShareGPT [8]\\\\nChatbot OPT-66B\\\\n132GB\\\\n2.5s\\\\n0.15s\\\\nShareGPT [8]\\\\nChatbot OPT-175B\\\\n350GB\\\\n4.0s\\\\n0.2s\\\\nShareGPT [8]\\\\nCode Completion OPT-66B\\\\n132GB\\\\n0.125s\\\\n0.2s\\\\nHumanEval [14]\\\\nSummarization OPT-66B\\\\n132GB\\\\n15s\\\\n0.15s\\\\nLongBench [13]\\\\nTable 1: Workloads in evaluation and latency requirements.\\\\n0\\\\n500\\\\n1000\\\\n1500\\\\n2000\\\\n# Tokens\\\\n0\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n6\\\\n8\\\\nDensity\\\\n1e\\\\n3\\\\nInput (avg=755.5)\\\\nOutput (avg=200.3)\\\\n0\\\\n500\\\\n1000\\\\n1500\\\\n2000\\\\n# Tokens\\\\n0\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n6\\\\n1e\\\\n3\\\\nInput (avg=171.3)\\\\nOutput (avg=98.2)\\\\n0\\\\n500\\\\n1000\\\\n1500\\\\n2000\\\\n# Tokens\\\\n0\\\\n5\\\\n10\\\\n15\\\\n1e\\\\n3\\\\nInput (avg=1738.3)\\\\nOutput (avg=90.7)\\\\n(a) ShareGPT\\\\n(b) HumanEval\\\\n(c) LongBench\\\\nFigure 7: The input and output length distributions of (a)\\\\nShareGPT, (b) HumanEval, and (c) LongBench datasets.\\\\nC++/CUDA code.\\\\nThe placement algorithm module implements the algorithm\\\\nand the simulator mentioned in §4 which gives the placement\\\\ndecision for a specific model and cluster setting. The fron-\\\\ntend supports an OpenAI API-compatible interface where\\\\nclients can specify the sampling parameters like maximum\\\\noutput length and temperature. The orchestration layer man-\\\\nages the prefill and decoding instances, responsible for request\\\\ndispatching, KV cache transmission, and results delivery. It\\\\nutilizes NCCL [6] for cross-node GPU communication and\\\\nasynchronous CudaMemcpy for intra-node communication,\\\\nwhich avoids blocking the GPU computation during transmis-\\\\nsion. Each instance is powered by a parallel execution engine,\\\\nwhich uses Ray [35] actor to implement GPU workers that\\\\nexecute the LLM inference and manage the KV Cache in\\\\na distributed manner. It integrates many recent LLM opti-\\\\nmizations like continuous batching [54], FlashAttention [20],\\\\nPagedAttention [32] and supports popular open-source LLMs\\\\nsuch as OPT [56] and LLaMA [51].\\\\n6\\\\nEvaluation\\\\nIn this section, we evaluate DistServe under different sizes\\\\nof LLMs ranging from 13B to 175B and various applica-\\\\ntion datasets including chatbot, code-completion, and sum-\\\\nmarization. The evaluation shows that DistServe consistently\\\\noutperforms the current state-of-the-art system across all the\\\\nsettings (§6.2). Specifically, DistServe can handle up to 7.4×\\\\nhigher rates and 12.6× more stringent SLO while meeting\\\\nthe latency requirements for over 90% requests. Addition-\\\\nally, we analyze the latency breakdown in DistServe to show\\\\nthe communication overhead is insubstantial thanks to our\\\\nbandwidth-aware placement algorithm (§6.3) and do abla-\\\\ntion studies of our techniques (§6.4). Finally, we profile the\\\\nexecution time of our placement algorithm (§6.5).\\\\n6.1\\\\nExperiments Setup\\\\nCluster testbed. We deploy DistServe on a cluster with 4\\\\nnodes and 32 GPUs. Each node has 8 NVIDIA SXM A100-\\\\n80GB GPUs connected with NVLINK. The cross-node band-\\\\nwidth is 25Gbps. Due to the limited cross-node bandwidth,\\\\nwe use the low node-affinity placement algorithm (§2) for\\\\nDistServe in most of the experiments except for the ablation\\\\nstudy (§6.4) which uses simulation.\\\\nModel and workloads setup. Similar to prior work on LLM\\\\nserving [32], we choose the OPT [56] model series, which\\\\nis a representative LLM family widely used in academia and\\\\nindustry. Newer GPT model families are adopting memory-\\\\nefficient attention mechanisms like GQA [10] and MQA [44].\\\\nDistServe will show better performance on these models be-\\\\ncause the transmission overhead is lower due to the decrease\\\\nin KV cache size. We choose OPT which uses the classic\\\\nMHA [52] to put enough pressure on the transmission over-\\\\nhead. We use FP16 precision in all experiments. For work-\\\\nloads, as shown in Table 1, We choose three typical LLM\\\\napplications and set the SLOs empirically based on their ser-\\\\nvice target because there exists no available SLO settings for\\\\nthese applications as far as we know. For each application,\\\\nwe select a suitable dataset and sample requests from it for\\\\nevaluation. Since all the datasets do not include timestamps,\\\\nwe generate request arrival times using Poisson distribution\\\\nwith different request rates. Due to the space limit, we test the\\\\nchatbot workload on all three OPT models and the other two\\\\nworkloads on OPT-66B, which matches the largest size in the\\\\nrecent open-source LLM series [51].\\\\n• Chatbot [1]: We use the ShareGPT dataset [8] for the\\\\nchatbot application, which is a collection of user-shared\\\\nconversations with ChatGPT. For OPT-13B, the TTFT SLO\\\\nis set to 0.25s for responsiveness and the TPOT SLO is\\\\nset to 0.1s which is higher than the normal human read\\\\nspeed. For OPT-66B and OPT-175B, we slightly relax the\\\\ntwo SLOs due to the increase in model execution latency.\\\\n• Code completion [14]: We use the HumanEval [14] dataset\\\\nfor the code completion task. It includes 164 programming\\\\nproblems with a function signature or docstring which is\\\\nused to evaluate the performance of code completion mod-\\\\nels. Since the code completion model is used as a personal\\\\nreal-time coding assistant, we set both SLOs to be stringent.\\\\n• Summarization [5]: It is a popular LLM task to generate\\\\na concise summary for a long article, essay, or even an\\\\nacademic paper. We use LongBench [13] dataset which\\\\ncontains the summarization task4. As shown in Figure 7,\\\\nLongBench has much longer input lengths than the other\\\\ntwo datasets. So we set a loose TTFT SLO but require a\\\\nstringent TPOT.\\\\nMetrics. We use SLO attainment as the major evaluation met-\\\\nric. We compare DistServe to two baseline systems:\\\\n• vLLM [32]: vLLM is a representative LLM serving sys-\\\\ntem widely used in both academia and industry. It sup-\\\\nports continuous batching [54] to increase throughput and\\\\npaged-attention [32] to reduce memory fragmentation dur-\\\\ning KV cache allocation. However, it colocates the prefill\\\\nand decoding computation to maximize the overall system\\\\nthroughput and struggles to meet the latency requirements\\\\ncost-efficiently. Since vLLM only supports intra-op paral-\\\\nlelism, we follow previous work [32] to set intra-op equals\\\\n1, 4, and 8 for the three OPT models, respectively.\\\\n• DeepSpeed-MII [3]: DeepSpeed Model Implementations\\\\nfor Inference (MII) supports chunked-prefill by decompos-\\\\ning long prompts into smaller chunks and composing with\\\\nshort prompts to exactly fill a target token budget. It miti-\\\\ngates but cannot eliminate the prefill-decoding interference\\\\ncaused by the long prefill job. We set its intra-op the same\\\\nas vLLM for OPT-13B and OPT-66B for a fair comparison.\\\\nHowever, DeepSpeed-MII cannot serve OPT-175B whose\\\\nvocab_size = 50272 because its underlying kernel imple-\\\\nmentation requires vocab_size/intra_op is a multiple of\\\\n8 where intra-op equals 8 does not satisfy. Setting intra-\\\\nop equals 4 can satisfy this requirement but will cause the\\\\nout-of-memory issue.\\\\n6.2\\\\nEnd-to-end Experiments\\\\nIn this Section, we compare the end-to-end performance of\\\\nDistServe against the baselines on real application datasets.\\\\nChatbot. We evaluate the performance of DistServe on the\\\\nchatbot application for all three OPT models. The first row\\\\nof Figure 8 illustrates that when we gradually increase the\\\\nrate, more requests will violate the latency requirements and\\\\nthe SLO attainment decreases. The vertical line shows the\\\\nmaximum per-GPU rate the system can handle to meet latency\\\\nrequirements for over 90% of the requests.\\\\nOn the ShareGPT dataset, DistServe can sustain 2.0×–\\\\n4.6× higher request rate compared to vLLM. This is because\\\\nDistLLM eliminates the prefill-decoding interference through\\\\ndisaggregation. Two phases can optimize their own objec-\\\\ntives by allocating different resources and employing tailored\\\\nparallelism strategies. Specifically, by analyzing the chosen\\\\nplacement strategy5 for 175B, we find the prefill instance\\\\nhas inter-op = 3, intra-op = 3; and the decoding instance has\\\\ninter-op = 3, intra-op = 4. Under this placement, DistServe\\\\ncan effectively balance the load between the two instances on\\\\nShareGPT, meeting latency requirements at the lowest cost.\\\\nThis non-trivial placement strategy is challenging to manu-\\\\nally find, proving the effectiveness of the algorithm. In the\\\\ncase of vLLM, collocating prefill and decoding greatly slows\\\\ndown the decoding phase, thereby significantly increasing\\\\nTPOT. Due to the stringent TPOT requirements of chatbot\\\\napplications, although vLLM meets the TTFT SLO for most\\\\nrequests, the overall SLO attainment is dragged down by a\\\\nlarge number of requests that violate the TPOT SLO. Com-\\\\npared to DeepSpeed-MII, DistServe can sustain 1.6×–7.4×\\\\nhigher request rate. DeepSpeed-MII shows better performance\\\\n5All the placements chosen by DistServe can be found in Appendix B.\\\\n10\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 11 ---\\\\n0.5\\\\n1.0\\\\n1.5\\\\n2.0\\\\nPer-GPU Rate (req/s)\\\\n0\\\\n50\\\\n100\\\\nSLO Attainment (%)\\\\n0.5\\\\n1.0\\\\n1.5\\\\nSLO Scale\\\\n0\\\\n50\\\\n100\\\\n0.2\\\\n0.4\\\\n0.6\\\\nPer-GPU Rate (req/s)\\\\n0\\\\n50\\\\n100\\\\n10\\\\n8\\\\n6\\\\n4\\\\n2\\\\nSLO Scale\\\\n0\\\\n50\\\\n100\\\\nDistServe\\\\nDeepSpeed-MII\\\\nvLLM\\\\n(a) Code Completion\\\\n(b) Summarization\\\\nFigure 9: Code completion and summarization tasks with OPT-66B on HumanEval and LongBench datasets, respectively.\\\\non larger models because the prefill job is larger and chunked-\\\\nprefill mitigates the interference to some extent. We divide the\\\\nprocessing lifecycle of a request in DistServe into five stages:\\\\nprefill queuing, prefill execution, transmission, decoding queu-\\\\ning, and decoding execution. The total time consumed by all\\\\nrequests in each stage is then summed up to determine their\\\\nrespective proportions in the system’s total execution time.\\\\nFigure 10(a) shows the latency breakdown for the OPT-\\\\n175B models on the ShareGPT dataset. This further demonstrates the importance\\\\nof disaggregation. The interference between the prefill and\\\\ndecoding phases significantly reduces the potential perfor-\\\\nmance improvement through adjusting parallelism. In con-\\\\ntrast, \\\\\\\"DistLLM-High\\\\\\\" can achieve further improvements over\\\\n\\\\\\\"DistLLM-Low\\\\\\\" because it is not constrained by the deploy-\\\\nment constraint that the prefill and decoding instance on one\\\\nnode should share the same model stage. Through disaggre-\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n8\\\\n16\\\\n32\\\\nThe number of GPUs\\\\n0\\\\n20\\\\n40\\\\n60\\\\n80\\\\nTime (s)\\\\nDistServe-Low\\\\nDistServe-High\\\\nFigure 12: Algorithm Running Time\\\\ngation, we can use tailored parallelism strategies for prefill\\\\nand decoding instances and optimize their targets without the\\\\ncoupling effects.\\\\n6.5\\\\nAlgorithm Running Time\\\\nFigure 12 shows the running time for Alg. 1 (DistServe-Low)\\\\nand Alg. 2 (DistServe-High) on an AWS m5d.metal instance\\\\nwith 96 cores as the number of GPUs (N ×M) provided to a\\\\nsingle instance increases. According to the results, DistServe\\\\nscales well with the number of GPUs and is independent of\\\\nthe model size. This is because the simulator only simulates\\\\ndiscrete events and the running time is the same no matter\\\\nhow big the model is. On the other hand, both algorithms are\\\\nhighly parallelizable, as the searches for different parallelism\\\\nstrategies are independent of each other, allowing the execu-\\\\ntion time of the algorithms to accelerate almost linearly with\\\\nmore CPU cores.\\\\nAs the number of GPUs increases, the execution time of\\\\n\\\\\\\"Dist-Low\\\\\\\" becomes higher than that of \\\\\\\"Dist-High\\\\\\\". This is\\\\nbecause the search for parallelism strategies for prefill and\\\\ndecoding instances in \\\\\\\"Dist-High\\\\\\\" is independent and can\\\\nbe parallelized. But for \\\\\\\"Dist-Low\\\\\\\", due to additional restric-\\\\ntions on deployment, we need to enumerate all the possible\\\\nintra-node parallelism combinations for prefill and decoding\\\\ninstances. Even so, the execution time of the algorithm is in\\\\nminutes, and since it only needs to be executed once before\\\\neach redeployment, this overhead is acceptable.\\\\n7\\\\nDiscussion\\\\nIn this paper, we focus on the goodput-optimized setting and\\\\npropose DistServe under the large-scale LLM serving sce-\\\\nnario. As LLMs are widely used and deployed across vari-\\\\nous service scenarios with different optimization targets and\\\\nresource limits, it becomes almost impossible to find a one-\\\\nsize-fits-all solution that effectively addresses all aspects of\\\\nLLM serving. In this section, we discuss the pros and cons of\\\\nDistServe and potentially better solutions in other scenarios.\\\\nThroughput-optimized scenarios. In offline applications\\\\nthat are not latency-sensitive, users typically have lower re-\\\\nquirements for response time [45]. This allows serving sys-\\\\ntems to shift focus towards maximizing overall throughput\\\\ninstead of goodput and the effectiveness of DistServe may be\\\\n12\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 13 ---\\\\ncompromised. In this case, techniques such as chunked-prefill\\\\nwith piggyback [3,9] may be preferred since it can fill each\\\\nbatch to the compute-bound threshold, thereby maintaining\\\\nhigher GPU utilization in every iteration.\\\\nResource-constrained scenarios. Small-scale enterprises\\\\nand individual researchers often lack the resources to deploy\\\\nLLMs on large-scale clusters [45,48]. In resource-constrained\\\\nscenarios, such as environments with only a few or even a\\\\nsingle GPU, the design space for DistServe is significantly\\\\nlimited. It struggles or even fails to adjust the parallel strate-\\\\ngies and resource allocation to effectively enhance serving\\\\nperformance. In this case, simpler architectural choices like\\\\nnon-disaggregated systems [3, 32] may reduce deployment\\\\ncomplexity and optimize operational efficiency.\\\\nLong-context scenarios. Nowadays, more and more GPT\\\\nmodels support extremely long contexts, such as Claude-\\\\n3 [11], Gemini-1.5 [22], and Large World Model (LWM) [34],\\\\nwhich all have a 1M context window. In such scenarios, the\\\\ntransmission overhead will increase as the size of the KV\\\\ncache grows linearly with the prompt length. However, the\\\\nprefill computation grows quadratically, so the relative dura-\\\\ntion of transmission and prefill job decreases. Meanwhile, a\\\\nlonger context further exacerbates the disparity in computa-\\\\ntional demands between prefill and decoding jobs, leading to\\\\nincreased interference between them. Therefore, the disaggre-\\\\ngation approach proposed in DistServe remains promising in\\\\nlong-context serving.\\\\n8\\\\nRelated Work\\\\nInference serving. There has been plenty of work on in-\\\\nference serving recently. They range from general-purpose\\\\nproduction-grade systems like TorchServe [7] and NVIDIA\\\\nTriton [19] to systems optimized specifically for Transformer-\\\\nbased LLMs [9, 18, 21, 33, 50, 53, 54, 60]. Among them,\\\\nOrca [54] introduces continuous batching to increase through-\\\\nput. vLLM [32] proposes paged-attention for fine-grained\\\\nKV cache management. SARATHI [9] suggests a chunked-\\\\nprefill approach, splitting a prefill request into chunks and\\\\npiggybacking decoding requests to improve hardware utiliza-\\\\ntion. FastServe [53] implements iteration-level preemptive\\\\nscheduling to mitigate the queuing delay caused by long jobs.\\\\nHowever, they all employ a colocation approach for prefill\\\\nand decoding processing, thus leading to severe interference.\\\\nThere are also concurrent works such as Splitwise [38], Tetri-\\\\nInfer [27] and DéjàVu [49] which adopt similar disaggregation\\\\nidea to optimize LLM inference, further confirming the ef-\\\\nfectiveness of this method. Differently, DistServe emphasizes\\\\nthe goodput optimization scenario more and takes a closer\\\\nlook at the aspect of network bandwidth.\\\\nGoodput-optimized systems. Optimizing goodput is a hot\\\\ntopic in DL applications. Pollux [39] improves scheduling\\\\nperformance in DL clusters by dynamically adjusting re-\\\\nsources for jobs to increase cluster-wide goodput. Sia [29]\\\\nintroduces a heterogeneous-aware scheduling approach that\\\\ncan efficiently match cluster resources to elastic resource-\\\\nadaptive jobs. Clockwork [23] and Shepherd [55] provide\\\\nlatency-aware scheduling and preemption to improve the serv-\\\\ning goodput, but they only target traditional small models.\\\\nAlpaServe [33] focuses on LLMs, employing model paral-\\\\nlelism to statistically multiplex the GPU execution thus im-\\\\nproving the resource utilization. However, it only targets the\\\\nnon-autoregressive generation. DistServe is the first work to\\\\noptimize the goodput for autoregressive LLM inference.\\\\nResource disaggregation. Resource disaggregated sys-\\\\ntems [17,25,43] decouple the hardware resources from the\\\\ntraditional monolithic server infrastructure and separate them\\\\ninto resource pools to manage independently. It allows for\\\\nmore flexible, efficient, and scalable deployment and increases\\\\nresource utilization. Many applications benefit from a truly\\\\ndisaggregated data center with high-speed network bandwidth\\\\nand heterogenous hardware support [12,30,57]. DistServe\\\\nshares the concept by disaggregating its system components,\\\\nallowing for independent resource scaling and management.\\\\nModel parallelism for training. DistServe is orthogonal\\\\nto the large body of work on model parallelism in train-\\\\ning [28,36,40,46,59]. As described in §3.3, inference-serving\\\\nworkloads have unique characteristics not found in training\\\\nsettings. Where these systems do intersect with DistServe, is\\\\nin their methods for implementing model parallelism along\\\\nvarious dimensions. DistServe can integrate new parallelism\\\\noptimizations into its placement searching algorithm.\\\\n9\\\\nConclusion\\\\nWe present DistServe, a new LLM serving architecture that\\\\ndisaggregates the prefill and decoding computation. DistServe\\\\nmaximizes the per-gpu goodput – the maximum request rate\\\\nthat can be served adhering to the SLO attainment goal for\\\\neach GPU provisioned, hence resulting in up to 7.4× lower\\\\ncost per LLM query with guaranteed satisfaction of SLOs.\\\\nOur findings affirm that as latency becomes an increasingly\\\\nimportant metric for LLM services, prefill and decoding dis-\\\\naggregation is a vital strategy in promising improved perfor-\\\\nmance and service quality guarantees.\\\\nAcknowledgments. Fast distribu\\\\n\\\\n[EXCERPT extracted-character range 80000:84000]\\\\nent\\\\nstrategies, we use an analytical model to predict the execution\\\\ntime of the prefill and decoding phases in LLM inference.\\\\nIn modern LLM serving systems [18, 32, 53], memory-\\\\nbound operations like Softmax and LayerNorm are usually\\\\nfused with matrix multiplication kernels for efficiency. Thus\\\\nthe GEMMs dominate the overall latency and our analysis\\\\nprimarily focuses on them.\\\\nA.1\\\\nSymbol Definition\\\\nHere are symbols related to the architecture of the model:\\\\n• h: hidden size\\\\n• n: number of heads\\\\n• s: head size (h = n·s)\\\\n• m: FFN intermediate size\\\\nNote: If tensor parallelism is used, h, n, and m should be\\\\ndivided by the tensor parallelism size.\\\\nBelow are symbols that characterize the batch to be exe-\\\\ncuted:\\\\n• B: batch size\\\\n• l0,l1,...,lB−1: input length of each request within the\\\\nbatch\\\\n• t: number of tokens in the batch, (t = ∑B−1\\\\ni=0 li)\\\\n• t2: squared sum of the input lengths (t2 = ∑B−1\\\\ni=0 l2\\\\ni )\\\\n• b: block size in the attention kernel. This parameter is\\\\nused in FlashAttention [20], a common kernel optimiza-\\\\ntion technique adopted by current LLM serving systems.\\\\nA.2\\\\nPrefill Phase Latency Modeling\\\\nSince the attention operation uses specially optimized kernels,\\\\nwe first discuss the other four matrix multiplications in the\\\\nprefill phase:\\\\nGEMM Name\\\\nShape of M\\\\nShape of N\\\\nQKV Linear\\\\n(t,h)\\\\n(h,3h)\\\\nAttn Output\\\\n(t,h)\\\\n(h,h)\\\\nFFN Input\\\\n(t,h)\\\\n(h,m)\\\\nFFN Output\\\\n(t,m)\\\\n(m,h)\\\\nThe arithmetic intensity (AI) of these operations is O(t).\\\\nOn NVIDIA A100-80GB GPU, it is compute-bound when AI\\\\nis over 156. Since t usually can reach several hundred in real\\\\ncases, all of these operations are compute-bound. Therefore,\\\\nwe can model the latency of these operations according to the\\\\ntotal FLOPs:\\\\nT1 = C1 ·(4th2 +2thm)\\\\nNext, we discuss the prefill attention operation with\\\\nFlashAttention [20] optimization. Since the attention only\\\\noperates among the tokens in the same request, current im-\\\\nplementations launch attention kernels for each request in\\\\nthe same batch. For one attention head and a request with\\\\nl tokens, the attention kernel needs to perform a total of\\\\n2sl +3sl ·(l/b) ≈3sl ·(l/b) memory reads and writes, along-\\\\nside 2sl2+sl(l/b) ≈2sl2 FLOPs. So the AI is 2b/3 = 10.677\\\\n(when b = 16) or 21.333 (when b = 32), indicating that it is\\\\na memory-bound operation on A100 GPU. Therefore, the\\\\nwhole attention layer latency (including all requests and all\\\\nheads) can be modeled as:\\\\nT2 = C2 ·n·\\\\nB−1\\\\n∑\\\\ni=0\\\\n3sl2\\\\ni\\\\nb\\\\n= C2 · 3nst2\\\\nb\\\\n= C2 · 3ht2\\\\nb\\\\nOverall, the latency of the prefill phase can be modeled as:\\\\nTPrefill = C1 ·(4th2 +2thm)+C2 · 3ht2\\\\nb\\\\n+C3\\\\nWe use C3 to quantify other overheads like Python Run-\\\\ntime, system noise, and so on. Then we use profiling and\\\\ninterpolation to figure out the values of C1, C2, and C3.\\\\nA.3\\\\nDecoding Phase Latency Modeling\\\\nSimilarly, we first focus on the following GEMMs in the\\\\ndecoding phase:\\\\nGEMM Name\\\\nShape of M\\\\nShape of N\\\\nQKV Linear\\\\n(B,h)\\\\n(h,3h)\\\\nAttn Output\\\\n(B,h)\\\\n(h,h)\\\\nFFN Input\\\\n(B,h)\\\\n(h,m)\\\\nFFN Output\\\\n(B,m)\\\\n(m,h)\\\\nThe AI of these operations is O(B). B is limited by the GPU\\\\nmemory size and stringent latency requirements, so in existing\\\\nserving scenarios, these operations are memory-bound. The\\\\ntotal memory reads and writes is 8Bh + 4h2 + 2hm + 2Bm,\\\\nand since h and m are usually significantly larger than B, we\\\\ncan model the latency as:\\\\nT3 = C4 ·(4h2 +2hm)\\\\nAs for the decoding attention operation, for one attention\\\\nhead and a request with l generated tokens, it needs to per-\\\\nform 3sl memory reads and writes, alongside 2sl FLOPs. It\\\\nis memory-bound, so we can model the latency of decoding\\\\nattention as:\\\\nT4 = C5 ·n·3s\\\\nB−1\\\\n∑\\\\ni=0\\\\nli = C5 ·3ht\\\\nSumming up, the latency of the decoding phase is:\\\\nTDecoding = C4 ·(4h2 +2hm)+C5 ·3ht\\\\nHere we do not introduce the overhead term (like C3 in the\\\\nprofiling stage) because 4h2 +2hm is already a constant, and\\\\nthe overhead can be put into C4. Similarly, we use profiling\\\\nand interpolation to figure out the values of C4 and C5.\\\\n17\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 18 ---\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n3\\\\nPer-GPU Rate (req/s)\\\\n0\\\\n50\\\\n100\\\\nSLO Attainment (%)\\\\n0.25\\\\n0.50\\\\n0.75\\\\n1.00\\\\nPer\\\", \\\"excerpt_ranges\\\": [[0, 20000], [24000, 78293], [80000, 84000]], \\\"range_unit\\\": \\\"zero-based half-open characters in extracted text\\\", \\\"extracted_characters\\\": 85689, \\\"selected_characters\\\": 78293, \\\"extraction\\\": \\\"UTF-8 text\\\", \\\"selection_reason\\\": \\\"Ranked 4000-character windows by current entry title/tags/questions and algorithm/mechanism keywords; ties retain source order.\\\"}, {\\\"path\\\": \\\"references/S-MLPERF-LLM/upstream/language/llama2-70b/README.md\\\", \\\"sha256\\\": \\\"f7eee4fb707a5035e7c8f8fe01f351a4620ea1ab904ca8086fcd9043eabb6b5e\\\", \\\"reading_scope\\\": \\\"full\\\", \\\"category\\\": \\\"source_original\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"# Reference Implementation for llama2-70b\\\\n\\\\n**Basic implementation for llama2-70b. command below:\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\n# First get the `open-orca` parquet from huggingface\\\\nexport OPENORCA_DATASET=${PWD}/open-orca\\\\ngit clone https://huggingface.co/datasets/Open-Orca/OpenOrca --export_dir=${EXPORT_DIR} --num_total_samples=24576\\\\n\\\\nmv ${EXPORT_DIR}/open_orca_gpt4_tokenized_llama.sampled_24576.pkl ${DATASET_PATH}\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThe script will perform the following steps on the original open_orca GPT4 dataset:\\\\n- filter out all queries with non-ascii characters, except for normal unicode quotes and hyphens.\\\\n- filter out all queries with out-of-bound output texts using Llama2 models\\\\n- sample equally from the sub-dataset (i.e. COT, NIV, FLAN, T0) and form the final dataset.\\\\n\\\\n## Run Performance Benchmarks\\\\n\\\\n### \\\"074479dbeb369205ccc8800450c647893b4901c247e0e4ee7f321f05254e9305\\\", \\\"reading_scope\\\": \\\"full\\\", \\\"category\\\": \\\"source_original\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"# Overview {#mainpage}\\\\n\\\\n## Introduction\\\\n\\\\n* The LoadGen is a *reusable* module that *efficiently* and *fairly* measures\\\\n  the performance of inference systems.\\\\n* It generates traffic for scenarios as formulated by a diverse set of experts\\\\n  in the [MLCommons working group](https://mlcommons.org/).\\\\n* The scenarios emulate the workloads seen in mobile devices,\\\\n  autonomous vehicles, robotics, and cloud-based setups.\\\\n* Although the LoadGen is not model or dataset aware, its strength is in its\\\\n  reusability with logic that is.\\\\n\\\\n## Integration Example and Flow\\\\nThe following is an diagram of how the LoadGen can be integrated into an\\\\ninference system, resembling how some of the MLPerf reference models are\\\\nimplemented.\\\\n<div style=\\\\\\\"display:flex; flex-flow:row wrap; justify-content: space-evenly;\\\\\\\">\\\\n<img src=\\\\\\\"https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mlcommons/inference/master/loadgen/loadgen_integration_diagram.svg\\\\\\\" width=\\\\\\\"500px\\\\\\\" style=\\\\\\\"padding: 20px\\\\\\\">\\\\n<ol style=\\\\\\\"padding: 20px\\\\\\\">\\\\n<li>Benchmark knows the model, dataset, and preprocessing.</li>\\\\n<li>Benchmark hands dataset sample IDs to LoadGen.</li>\\\\n<li>LoadGen starts generating queries of sample IDs.</li>\\\\n<li>Benchmark creates requests to backend.</li>\\\\n<li>Result is post processed and forwarded to LoadGen.</li>\\\\n<li>LoadGen outputs logs for analysis.<br>\\\\n</ol>\\\\n</div>\\\\n\\\\n## Useful Links\\\\n* [FAQ](README_FAQ.md)\\\\n* [LoadGen Build Instructions](README_BUILD.md)\\\\n* [LoadGen API](loadgen.h)\\\\n* [Test Settings](test_settings.h) -\\\\n  A good description of available scenarios, modes, and knobs.\\\\n* [MLPerf Inference Code](https://github.com/mlcommons/inference) -\\\\n  Includes source for the LoadGen and reference models that use the LoadGen.\\\\n* [MLPerf Inference Rules](https://github.com/mlcommons/inference_policies) -\\\\n  Any mismatch with this is a bug in the LoadGen.\\\\n\\\\n## Scope of the LoadGen's Responsibilities\\\\n\\\\n### In Scope\\\\n* **Provide a reusable** C++ library with python bindings.\\\\n* **Implement** the traffic patterns of the MLPerf Inference scenarios and\\\\n  modes.\\\\n* **Record** all traffic generated and received for later analysis and\\\\n  verification.\\\\n* **Summarize** the results and whether performance constraints were met.\\\\n* **Target high-performance** systems with efficient multi-thread friendly\\\\n  logging utilities.\\\\n* **Generate trust** via a shared, well-tested, and community-hardened\\\\n  code base.\\\\n\\\\n### Out of Scope\\\\nThe LoadGen is:\\\\n* **NOT** aware of the ML model it is running against.\\\\n* **NOT** aware of the data formats of the model's inputs and outputs.\\\\n* **NOT** aware of how to score the accuracy of a model's outputs.\\\\n* **NOT** aware of MLPerf rules regarding scenario-specific constraints.\\\\n\\\\nLimitting the scope of the LoadGen in this way keeps it reusable across\\\\ndifferent models and datasets without modification. Using composition and\\\\ndependency injection, the user can define their own model, datasets, and\\\\nmetrics.\\\\n\\\\nAdditionally, not hardcoding MLPerf-specific test constraints, like test\\\\nduration and performance targets, allows users to use the LoadGen unmodified\\\\nfor custom testing and continuous integration purposes.\\\\n\\\\n## Submission Considerations\\\\n\\\\n### Upstream all local modifications\\\\n* As a rule, no local modifications to the LoadGen's C++ library are allowed\\\\nfor submission.\\\\n* Please upstream early and often to keep the playing field level.\\\\n\\\\n### Choose your TestSettings carefully!\\\\n* Since the LoadGen is oblivious to the model, it can't enforce the MLPerf\\\\nrequirements for submission. *e.g.:* target percentiles and latencies.\\\\n* For verification, the values in TestSettings are logged.\\\\n* To help make sure your settings are spec compliant, use\\\\nTestSettings::FromConfig in conjunction with the relevant config file provided\\\\nwith the reference models.\\\\n\\\\n## Responsibilities of a LoadGen User\\\\n\\\\n### Implement the Interfaces\\\\n* Implement the SystemUnderTest and QuerySampleLibrary interfaces and pass\\\\n  them to the StartTest function.\\\\n* Call QuerySampleComplete for every sample received by\\\\n  SystemUnderTest::IssueQuery.\\\\n\\\\n### Assess Accuracy\\\\n* Process the *mlperf_log_accuracy.json* output by the LoadGen to determine\\\\n  the accuracy of your system.\\\\n* For the official models, Python scripts will be provided by the MLPerf model\\\\n  owners for you to do this automatically.\\\\n\\\\nFor templates of how to do the above in detail, refer to code for the demos,\\\\ntests, and reference models.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## LoadGen over the Network\\\\n\\\\nFor reference, on a high level a submission looks like this:\\\\n\\\\n<div align=\\\\\\\"center\\\\\\\" style=\\\\\\\"display:flex; flex-flow:row wrap; justify-content: space-evenly;\\\\\\\">\\\\n<img src=\\\\\\\"https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mlcommons/inference/master/loadgen/diagram_submission.png\\\\\\\" width=\\\\\\\"300px\\\\\\\" style=\\\\\\\"padding: 20px\\\\\\\">\\\\n</div>\\\\n\\\\nThe LoadGen implementation is common to all submissions, while the QSL (“Query Sample Library”) and SUT (“System Under Test”) are implemented by submitters. QSL is responsible for loading the data and includes untimed preprocessing.\\\\n\\\\nA submission over the network introduces a new component “QDL” (query dispatch library) that is added to the system as presented in the following diagram:\\\\n\\\\n<div align=\\\\\\\"center\\\\\\\" style=\\\\\\\"display:flex; flex-flow:row wrap; justify-content: space-evenly;\\\\\\\">\\\\n<img src=\\\\\\\"https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mlcommons/inference/master/loadgen/diagram_network_submission.png\\\\\\\" width=\\\\\\\"300px\\\\\\\" style=\\\\\\\"padding: 20px\\\\\\\">\\\\n</div>\\\\n\\\\nQDL is a proxy for a load-balancer, that dispatches queries to SUT over a physical network, receives the responses and passes them back to LoadGen.  It is implemented by the submitter. The interface of the QDL is the same as the API to SUT. \\\\n\\\\nIn scenarios using QDL, data may be compressed in QSL at the choice of the submitter in order to reduce network transmission time. Decompression is part of the timed processing in SUT. A set of approved standard compression schemes will be specified for each benchmark; additional compression schemes must be approved in advance by the Working Group.\\\\n\\\\nAll communication between LoadGen/QSL and SUT is via QDL, and all communication between QDL and SUT must pass over a physical network.\\\\n\\\\nQDL implements the protocol to transmit queries over the network and receive responses. It also implements decompression of any response returned by the SUT, where compression of responses is allowed. Performing any part of the timed preprocessing or inference in QDL is specifically disallowed. Currently no batching is allowed in QDL, although this may be revisited in future.\\\\n\\\\nThe MLperf over the Network will run in Server mode and Offline mode. All LoadGen modes are expected to work as is with insignificant changes. These include running the test in performance mode, accuracy mode, find peak performance mode and compliance mode. The same applies for power measurements.\\\\n\\\\n### QDL details\\\\nThe Query Dispatch Library is implemented by the submitter and interfaces with LoadGen using the same SUT API. All MLPerf Inference SUTs implement the `mlperf::SystemUnderTest` class which is defined in system_under_test.h. The QDL implements `mlperf::QueryDispatchLibrary` class which inherits the `mlperf::SystemUnderTest` class and has the same API and support all existing `mlperf::SystemUnderTest` methods. It has a separate header file query_dispatch_library.h. Using sut with `mlperf::SystemUnderTest` class in LoadGen StartTest is natively upcasting `mlperf::QueryDispatchLibrary` class.\\\\n\\\\n#### QDL Query issue and response over the network\\\\n\\\\nThe QDL gets the queries from the LoadGen through \\\\n```CPP\\\\nvoid IssueQuery(const std::vector<QuerySample>& samples)\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThe QDL dispatches the queries to the SUT over the physical media. The exact method and implementation for it are submitter specific and would not be specified at MLCommons. Submitter implementation includes all methods required to serialize the query, load balance, drive it to the Operating system and network interface card and send to the SUT.\\\\n\\\\nThe QDL receives the query responses over the network from the SUT. The exact method and implementation for it are submitter specific and would not be specified at MLCommons. The submitter implementation includes all methods required to receive the network data from the Network Interface card, go through the Operating system, deserialize the query response, and provide it back to the LoadGen through query completion by:\\\\n\\\\n```CPP\\\\nstruct QuerySampleResponse {\\\\n  ResponseId id;\\\\n  uintptr_t data;\\\\n  size_t size;\\\\n};\\\\nvoid QuerySamplesComplete(QuerySampleResponse* responses, \\\\n                          size_t response_count);\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n#### QDL Additional Methods\\\\n\\\\nIn addition to that the QDL needs to implement the following methods that are provided by the SUT interface to the LoadGen:\\\\n```CPP\\\\nconst std::string& Name();\\\\n```\\\\nThe `Name` function returns a known string for over the Network SUTs to identify it as over the network benchmark.\\\\n```CPP\\\\nvoid FlushQueries();\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nIt is not specified here how the QDL would query and configure the SUT to execute the above methods. The QDL responds to the LoadGen after receiving its own response from the SUT.\\\\n\\\\n### Example\\\\n\\\\nRefer to [LON demo](demos/lon) for a reference example illustrating usage of Loadgen over the network.\\\\n\\\\n## Find Peak Performance Mode\\\\n\\\\nThe Find Peak Performance mode can be used to find the optimal queries per second (QPS) for the server scenario.\\\\n\\\\n### Setup\\\\n\\\\nYou can setup loadgen to run this mode by setting the `mode` variable in the `test_settings` used to run the test. Using the Python API:\\\\n\\\\n```python\\\\nsettings = mlperf_loadgen.TestSettings()\\\\nsettings.server_target_qps = 100\\\\nsettings.scenario = mlperf_loadgen.TestScenario.Server\\\\nsettings.mode = mlperf_loadgen.TestMode.FindPeakPerformance\\\\n...\\\\n\\\\nmlperf_loadgen.StartTest(sut, qsl, settings)\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nUsing the C/C++ API:\\\\n```CPP\\\\nmlperf::TestSettings settings;\\\\nsetting.server_target_qps = 100;\\\\nsettings.scenario = mlperf::TestScenario::Server;\\\\nsettings.mode = mlperf::TestMode::FindPeakPerformance;\\\\nmlperf::LogSettings log_settings;\\\\n/*\\\\nConstruct QSL and SUT\\\\n*/\\\\nmlperf::StartTest(&sut, &qsl, settings, log_settings);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n**Note:** Make sure you are setting the TestScenario to server and you are providing an initial target QPS.\\\\n\\\\n### Description\\\\n\\\\nThe Find Peak Performance mode works by finding a lower and upper boundary for the optimal QPS. Then performing a binary search between the lower and upper bound to find the optimal QPS.\\\\n\\\\n#### Finding lower and upper boundary\\\\n\\\\nLoadGen begins by running performance mode at the specified target QPS. If the test passes, this value is used as the lower bound; otherwise, an error is raised. The algorithm then guesses the upper bound as twice the target QPS. \\\\n\\\\nThen LoadGen will run performance mode using the upper bound guess. If the test is successful, both the lower bound and upper bound will be doubled. This repeats until the upper bound guess fails the test.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\n[initial_target_qps, 2*initial_target_qps] -> [2*initial_target_qps, 4*initial_target_qps] -> [4*initial_target_qps, 8*initial_target_qps]...\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nFinally, the final lower bound and upper bound are set to their current values. This process assures that the lower bound passes the performance mode, but the upper bound doesn’t.\\\\n\\\\n#### Binary Search\\\\n\\\\nOnce the lower and upper bounds are set, binary search can be performed over the range `[lower, upper]`` to find the optimal QPS. If a given QPS fails in performance mode, the optimal value lies below it; if it passes, the optimal is higher.\\\\n\\\", \\\"excerpt_ranges\\\": [[0, 11382]], \\\"range_unit\\\": \\\"zero-based half-open characters in extracted text\\\", \\\"extracted_characters\\\": 11382, \\\"selected_characters\\\": 11382, \\\"extraction\\\": \\\"UTF-8 text\\\", \\\"selection_reason\\\": \\\"full extracted text fits allocation\\\"}, {\\\"path\\\": \\\"references/S-SERVERLESSLLM/fulltext.txt\\\", \\\"sha256\\\": \\\"8fb94782eb4bf30cd44f72b99bbf5adc5ee88c9ae831a29d0ad604fb99f3e4c3\\\", \\\"reading_scope\\\": \\\"excerpt\\\", \\\"category\\\": \\\"source_original\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"[EXCERPT extracted-character range 0:70292]\\\\n=== PDF page 1 ===\\\\nServerlessLLM: Locality-Enhanced Serverless Inference for Large Language Models\\\\nYao Fu1 Leyang Xue1 Yeqi Huang1 Andrei-Octavian Brabete1 Dmitrii Ustiugov2 Yuvraj Patel1 Luo Mai1\\\\n1The University of Edinburgh\\\\n2NTU Singapore\\\\nAbstract\\\\nThis paper presents ServerlessLLM, a locality-enhanced\\\\nserverless inference system for Large Language Models\\\\n(LLMs). ServerlessLLM exploits the substantial capacity and\\\\nbandwidth of storage and memory devices available on GPU\\\\nservers, thereby reducing costly remote checkpoint downloads\\\\nand achieving efficient checkpoint loading. ServerlessLLM\\\\nachieves this through three main contributions: (i) fast LLM\\\\ncheckpoint loading via a novel loading-optimized checkpoint\\\\nformat design, coupled with an efficient multi-tier checkpoint\\\\nloading system; (ii) locality-driven LLM inference with live\\\\nmigration, which allows ServerlessLLM to effectively achieve\\\\nlocality-driven server allocation while preserving the low la-\\\\ntency of ongoing LLM inference; and (iii) locality-aware\\\\nserver allocation, enabling ServerlessLLM to evaluate the sta-\\\\ntus of each server in a cluster and effectively schedule model\\\\nstartup time to capitalize on local checkpoint placement. Our\\\\ncomprehensive experiments, which include microbenchmarks\\\\nand real-world traces, show that ServerlessLLM surpasses\\\\nstate-of-the-art systems by 10 - 200X in latency performance\\\\nwhen running various LLM inference workloads.\\\\n1\\\\nIntroduction\\\\nLarge Language Models (LLMs) have recently been incor-\\\\nporated into various online applications, including program-\\\\nming assistants [23], search engines [16], and conversational\\\\nbots [51]. These applications process user inputs, like ques-\\\\ntions, by breaking them down into tokens (e.g., words). LLMs\\\\nrespond in an autoregressive fashion, predicting each subse-\\\\nquent token based on the combination of input tokens and\\\\nthose generated so far, until a sentence-ending token (EoS) is\\\\nreached. To streamline this process, LLMs employ key-value\\\\ncaches to store intermediate results, reducing the need for\\\\nrepeated computations.\\\\nServing LLM inference at scale is a challenging problem,\\\\ngiven the substantial GPU resources it requires and the low\\\\nresponse time constraints such interactive services need to\\\\nsatisfy. Furthermore, LLM inference latency is difficult to\\\\npredict because their response time depends on the output\\\\nlength, which can vary significantly [24,39,77], due to iter-\\\\native output token generation. To achieve low latency, pro-\\\\ncessing an LLM request often necessitates the use of several\\\\nGPUs for durations ranging from seconds to minutes. In prac-\\\\ntice, LLM service providers need to host a large number of\\\\nLLMs catered to different developers, leading to significant\\\\nGPU consumption [15] and impeding the sustainability of\\\\nLLM services [19]. As a result, LLM inference services have\\\\nto impose strict caps on the number of requests sent to their\\\\nservices from their users (e.g., 40 messages per 3 hours for\\\\nChatGPT [51]), showing the provider’s current inability to\\\\nsatisfy the LLM inference demand. Researchers [19] project\\\\nthat LLM inference costs may increase by > 50× when it\\\\nreaches the popularity of Google Search.\\\\nTo reduce GPU consumption, LLM service providers are\\\\nexploring serverless inference, as seen in systems like Ama-\\\\nzon SageMaker [60], Azure [46], KServe [11] and Hugging-\\\\nFace [31]. In such setup, developers upload their LLM check-\\\\npoints, including model execution files and model parameter\\\\nfiles, to a storage system. Upon receiving a request, the system\\\\nuses a model loading scheduler to allocate available GPUs for\\\\nstarting up these checkpoints. A request router then directs\\\\nthe inference request to the selected GPUs. Using serverless\\\\nmethod enables providers to efficiently multiplex LLMs on\\\\nshared GPUs, enhancing utilization. Additionally, it offers\\\\ncost benefits to the developers, who pay only per request pro-\\\\ncessed, avoiding the expense of long-term GPU reservations.\\\\nWhile serverless inference holds promise for LLMs, it intro-\\\\nduces significant latency overheads. LLM checkpoints, which\\\\nrange from gigabytes [4,72,86] to terabytes [26] in size due to\\\\ntheir significant number of parameters, incur considerable de-\\\\nlays when downloaded from remote storage. Moreover, these\\\\ncheckpoints consist of numerous tensors, each with varying\\\\nstructures and sizes. The process of loading tensors onto\\\\nGPUs (often involving file deserialisation, memory allocation,\\\\ntensor shape parsing, and more) further contributes to delays.\\\\nWe aim to enhance locality in serverless inference for\\\\n1\\\\narXiv:2401.14351v1  [cs.LG]  25 Jan 2024\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 2 ===\\\\nLLMs. Notably, GPU-based inference servers feature multi-\\\\ntier storage architecture which has substantial host memory\\\\nand storage capabilities, yet these resources are underutilized\\\\nin systems like KServe [11] and Ray Serve [68]. Typically,\\\\nonly part of the host memory is used during model inference,\\\\nand SSDs are minimally employed for caching checkpoints\\\\ndownloaded from the model repository. This underutiliza-\\\\ntion led us to a new system design approach: leveraging the\\\\nmulti-tier storage architecture for local checkpoint storage\\\\nand utilizing their significant storage bandwidth for efficient\\\\ncheckpoint loading.\\\\nHowever, this design approach raises several open concerns:\\\\n(i) Given the complex storage architecture of a GPU server,\\\\nwhich includes multiple GPUs, DRAM, SSDs, and remote\\\\nstorage, all interconnected through various connections like\\\\nPCIe, NVMe and networks, how can we optimize LLM check-\\\\npoint loading to fully leverage the available bandwidth? (ii)\\\\nOpting for servers with pre-loaded checkpoints can improve\\\\nlocality in serverless inference systems, but this might cause\\\\nGPU contention because these servers have ongoing LLM\\\\ninferences with unpredictable completion times. How do we\\\\neffectively handle such GPU contention? (iii) In a distributed\\\\ncluster tasked with loading a model for request processing,\\\\nwhat strategy should be employed to select GPUs to minimize\\\\nthe latency of starting up the model?\\\\nTo address the above, we introduce ServerlessLLM, a\\\\nlocality-enhanced serverless inference system for LLMs. We\\\\nmake several contributions in designing ServerlessLLM:\\\\n(1) Fast LLM checkpoint loading. ServerlessLLM can max-\\\\nimize the storage bandwidth usage of GPU servers for LLM\\\\ncheckpoint loading. It introduces (i) a new loading-optimized\\\\ncheckpoint that supports sequential, chunk-based reading and\\\\nefficient tensor in-memory addressing, and (ii) an efficient\\\\nmulti-tier checkpoint loading system that can harness the sub-\\\\nstantial capacity and bandwidth on a multi-tier memory hier-\\\\narchy, through an in-memory data chunk pool, memory-copy-\\\\nefficient data path, and a multi-stage data loading pipeline.\\\\n(2) Locality-driven LLM inference with live migration. We\\\\nmotivate the need for live migration of LLM inference and\\\\nare the first to implement LLM live migration in serverless\\\\ninference systems to enhance the performance when support-\\\\ning locality-driven inference. The live migration is realized\\\\nusing two new mechanisms: (i) efficient token-based migra-\\\\ntion which determines the smallest necessary set of tokens\\\\nfor accurately moving LLM inference to another server, and\\\\n(ii) two-stage live migration enabling the transfer of LLM\\\\ninference without impacting the user experience in online\\\\napplications.\\\\n(3) Locality-aware server allocation. ServerlessLLM aids\\\\nthe model loading scheduler in serverless inference systems\\\\nby enabling latency-preserving, locality-driven server selec-\\\\ntion. It integrates models for accurately estimating the time\\\\nof loading checkpoints from different tiers in the storage hier-\\\\nNode 1 (Warm)\\\\nLLM Instance 1\\\\nController\\\\nInference \\\\nRequest\\\\nKV cache\\\\nRequest \\\\nRouter\\\\nModel \\\\nLoading \\\\nScheduler\\\\nStart-up request\\\\nModel\\\\nStorage\\\\nRoute\\\\nAllocate\\\\nLocal storage\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\nNode 2 (Cold)\\\\nLLM Instance 2\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\nLocal storage\\\\nLLM\\\\n…\\\\nEOS?\\\\nInput tokens\\\\nOutput tokens\\\\nNext token Yes\\\\nNo\\\\nDownload\\\\nFigure 1: Overview of LLM serverless inference systems\\\\narchy and the time of migrating an LLM inference to another\\\\nserver. Based on the estimation results, ServerlessLLM can\\\\nchoose the best server to minimize model startup latency.\\\\nIn our comprehensive evaluation of ServerlessLLM, we\\\\ncompared it against various baseline methods for running\\\\ndiverse LLM inference workloads in a GPU cluster. Micro-\\\\nbenchmark tests reveal that ServerlessLLM’s rapid LLM\\\\ncheckpoint loading significantly outperforms existing systems\\\\nlike Safetensors [32], and PyTorch [56], achieving 3.6-8.2X\\\\nfaster loading time performance. This is particularly notable\\\\nwith models such as OPT [86], LLaMA-2 [72], and Falcon [4].\\\\nFinally, we evaluated ServerlessLLM with real-world\\\\nserverless\\\\nworkloads, modelled on\\\\nthe\\\\npublic Azure\\\\nTrace [61], and benchmarked it against KServe, Ray Serve,\\\\nand a Ray Serve variant with local checkpoint caching.
